description:
Somos estudiantes de ciencia de datos de la Universidad Tecnológica de Bolívar interesados en el aprendizaje y experiencia de la hackathon de la nasa.

Nuestros fuertes son el análisis de datos, la visualización de datos, iteración de modelos y el desarrollo de software.
summary:
Fintrax is a health-monitoring software designed for the conditions astronauts face during long-duration spaceflight missions, such as those aboard the International Space Station.

Each astronaut is assigned an ID and records their baseline health parameters while at rest and in good health. Fintrax then compares mission measurements and reported symptoms against that personal baseline, classifies risk as low, medium, or high, and screens for signs of space-related conditions, from physical to cognitive.

Built as a PWA that also works offline, Fintrax helps astronauts track their health throughout the mission. Beyond flagging possible issues, it sends alerts to the appropriate roles (such as the flight physician) and provides recommendations based on the NEWS2 (National Early Warning Score 2) and NASA technical documentation.

Fintrax is a prototype: it does not diagnose or replace a flight physician.
details:
Fintrax is an innovative health monitoring software prototype created to support astronauts during short- and long-duration spaceflights and missions, in which they may experience effects such as space radiation, changes in gravity, isolation, confinement, and other demanding environmental conditions that can affect their lives. This project took into account that immediate medical support is not always available when needed during a space mission. For this reason, our team developed a system that allows astronauts to review and monitor their physiological conditions, enabling them to identify possible health risks and understand more effectively the changes their bodies undergo through this personalized, interactive, accessible, and easy-tounderstand system. In this way, Fintrax not only provides a vital signs system, but also seeks to transform physiological information into meaningful assessments that help astronauts make decisions based on their well-being.

What we did was develop a system in which the astronaut first records their vital signs while inactive and in good health. This is important because it gives us a reference for how their body normally functions and, once they are on the mission, allows us to compare those values with the new data they enter. They can also indicate what symptoms they have or how they are feeling at that moment. With this new information, Fintrax performs an assessment using NEWS2, a system that serves as the basis for classifying risk as low, medium, or high. In addition, we take into account how much the measurements have changed compared with the initial values and certain environmental factors, such as carbon dioxide inside the cabin. We also included a review of eight areas related to health problems that may occur in space. All of this is displayed on the page through graphs, results, and an astronaut avatar that represents the condition of their organs. The idea is that they do not have to interpret a large number of figures on their own, but can more easily understand what the system is showing.

We have also taken into account from the beginning that not all astronauts are physically alike. For this reason, we have added fields such as sex, height, and weight. We have also included certain physiological aspects related to the menstrual cycle. Likewise, we have added alerts that highlight concerning values or values that persist over time. This makes it easier for astronauts to monitor their health and know when they should pay closer attention to how they feel. On the other hand, since this is personal information, we have also included access controls to prevent just any user from viewing all the information.

As for programming, the project was divided into two parts. For the backend, we worked with Python and FastAPI (where the data is handled and calculations are performed); this is where measurements were compared and the risk level was obtained. For the frontend, we worked with JavaScript, HTML, and CSS. The page was created so that users could interact with it. They could enter their data and consult the results. Both parts were connected through an API. This allowed the data entered into the interface to be sent to the backend for evaluation. Different artificial intelligence tools were used, such as ChatGPT, Claude, OpenCode, Claude Code, Gemini, DeepSeek, and Big Pickle. We gradually defined what we wanted and how it would work. These tools helped us with different programming-related tasks (error checking, code organization, etc.). Tests were carried out in Python and Node.js. We checked that the API worked (using Uvicorn and curl). Git was also used to keep track of changes.

One of the areas we have worked on most is how we present the information. We wanted to prevent Fintrax from becoming just an input-and-output form. For this reason, we incorporated graphical elements and used an avatar to show the condition of the organs. In this way, we make the information easier to understand for people who are not medical experts. We have also worked to make these assessments adaptive. In other words, to use parameters based on each astronaut's usual values instead of universal parameters. In this case, we had to think about what information we need, how to structure the website, how to handle personal data, and how reliable the parameters we are using are. For this reason, we have taken scientific documentation into account. It should be noted that some of these values require adjustments and validation by experts.

The objective of this project is to offer a possible solution to the problem of monitoring astronauts' health in environments far from Earth, which future space missions will have to face. We know that there are aspects of Fintrax that can be improved. It should not be considered a substitute for a doctor. Nor can it be used as a diagnostic tool (that would require many more tests and validations). Nevertheless, we have managed to create a prototype that integrates different monitoring functions into a single application. In this way, the information can be handled in a more structured manner. What matters about Fintrax is that it tries to address a real problem with the tools available to us. It is a foundation on which to continue working toward a more practical approach to health in space missions.
